output.brief: The gap is mostly a tenure effect, not a location effect. Only 32% of remote staff had 18 months in their level at the census date, against 74% of office staff, because remote hiring opened widely only in July 2024. Among eligible employees, nomination, approval and promotion rates are almost the same: 20.0% remote against 21.1% office. Applying office rates to the remote tenure mix predicts 8.2%, and the observed rate is 7.6%. The gap is not explained by job family, since the gap shows in every family. Remote staff are not leaving at higher rates either. Proximity bias is not shown by this data, though the eligible remote group is small (110), so a modest real difference can't be ruled out. The manager comments about handing urgent work to nearby staff hint at a possible stretch-assignment issue, but that is untested. I'd not announce the three-day office rule. It would penalize about 180 people hired on home-based contracts and rests on a misread of the data. Put it on hold, report promotion rates for eligible employees only, and re-check at FY2027. Consider collecting staffing data on stretch assignments, and clarify promotion criteria for remote staff. I'm fairly confident (about 80%) in this reading.
